sources.title: Estudio de vulnerabilidad y riesgo de pueblos indígenas de Chile ante el cambio climático
sources.temporal_coverage: Consultancy report dated 10 April 2024; combines literature and participant workshops on Indigenous climate vulnerability, adaptation and risk.
sources.methodology: Consultancy report combining literature and Mapuche workshops.
sources.limitations: Proposed input, not official policy; Indigenous-specific indicators lack public disaggregated data.

sources.title: Emergency: Wildfires in Chile. Humanitarian Flash Note No. 2
sources.temporal_coverage: Humanitarian situation and response during central and southern Chile wildfires, February–7 March 2024.
sources.methodology: UNICEF flash report using official event data and a 44-interview rapid assessment in Viña del Mar.
sources.limitations: Emergency snapshot; report does not attribute fires to climate change.

sources.title: Chile ya cuenta con su primer Plan de Adaptación al Cambio Climático para los Recursos Hídricos
sources.organization: Dirección General de Aguas, Ministry of Public Works (Chile)
sources.temporal_coverage: DGA account published 28 September 2026 on the formal water-sector adaptation plan and implementation tools.
sources.methodology: Agency page summarizing formal plan status, measures, pilot indicators and local capacity-building.
sources.limitations: Describes plan inputs and implementation activities, not evaluated hydrological or household outcomes.

sources.title: Resolución Exenta N° 244: Procedimiento de consulta previa y convocatoria a instituciones representativas del pueblo Mapuche
sources.organization: Ministry of Social Development and Family, Subsecretariat of Social Services; Diario Oficial de Chile
sources.temporal_coverage: Resolution published 3 July 2025; recitals summarize the Peace and Understanding Commission mandate and land-fund information through 2024.
sources.methodology: Official resolution and recitals presenting the government's territorial-conflict framing, commission mandate and administrative land-fund data.
sources.limitations: Official administrative framing, not an independent violence dataset or evaluation of conflict-resolution outcomes.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 68–69, Mapuche territorial identities and livelihoods
claims.paraphrase: The study places Lafkenche communities in coastal Carahue, Puerto Saavedra, Toltén and Teodoro Schmidt; Wenteche farming communities lie along the Cautín and Quepe rivers.
claims.limitations: Livelihood description, not an exposure count.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 71–72, Mapuche conceptual impact chain; p. 75, Table 2.8
claims.paraphrase: Workshop participants link declining precipitation to lower groundwater recharge and saline-intrusion risk in coastal wells; rural households may rely on water trucks if rural systems fail.
claims.scenario: Conceptual workshop chain; no emissions scenario or period specified.
claims.limitations: Workshop pathway, not a quantified local risk estimate.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 71–72, Mapuche workshop and conceptual impact chain
claims.paraphrase: The study reports Mapuche–forestry-company land disputes and conflicts over culturally significant sites, biodiversity and water sources.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: It traces land disputes to overlapping Mapuche titles and historical transfers to forestry firms; it does not claim climate change causes these disputes.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 74, 81–82, Mapuche adaptation capacities and proposed measures
claims.paraphrase: Participants identify community organization, territorial knowledge, medicinal plants and seed-saving as adaptation capacities; culturally appropriate rural water systems and government coordination are proposed.
claims.limitations: Water-service and coordination measures are proposals, not evaluated outcomes.

claims.locator: PDF p. 1, situation overview and fire impacts
claims.paraphrase: February 2024 fires affected six regions; Valparaíso had 14,954 ha damaged and 6,587 homes destroyed; FIBE recorded 4,163 severely affected children.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 1–2, Child Protection Rapid Assessment
claims.paraphrase: UNICEF interviewed 44 people in 14 Viña del Mar locations; leading reported needs were protection, waste collection and drinking water.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 1, 4–5, emergency displacement and protection findings
claims.paraphrase: After the fires, UNICEF documented family separation/displacement; over half of respondents cited drug/alcohol-related local security problems, and 16% perceived physical/sexual violence.
claims.limitations: Rapid-interview findings, not prevalence or conflict data.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: UNICEF links post-fire displacement to protection risk; reported violence is not labeled conflict-related.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 1–2, 5, emergency coordination and water response
claims.paraphrase: Fire damage caused water cuts; emergency taps/tanks were installed, but UNICEF noted coordination problems and water shortages for cooking and washing.

claims.locator: HTML, paragraph on national water-security challenges
claims.paraphrase: DGA reports 2022 public-network drinking-water coverage of 99.9% in urban areas versus 57% of the rural population; irrigated agriculture and livestock account for about 73% of consumptive demand.
claims.limitations: National aggregate and demand shares; no subnational or Indigenous disaggregation.

claims.locator: HTML, paragraphs on formal PACC-RH status and plan measures
claims.paraphrase: Chile's formal water-sector adaptation plan has 10 measures and 35 actions for urban/rural water and sanitation, ecosystems, productive water use, territorial planning, knowledge and preparedness for droughts and floods.
claims.limitations: Approved measures and plans do not establish effectiveness or completed outcomes.

claims.locator: HTML, paragraphs on pilot basin indicators and municipal water-action kit
claims.paraphrase: The plan's implementation developed 38 basin-security indicators piloted in Camiña, Maipo, Valdivia and Seno Andrew with 195 participants; a municipal water-action kit reached representatives of more than 170 municipalities.
claims.limitations: Pilot development and training reach are not evidence of improved water security.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 3–4, recitals 8°–12° on the Peace and Understanding Commission
claims.paraphrase: The resolution locates the historic Mapuche–State territorial conflict mainly in Biobío, La Araucanía, Los Ríos and Los Lagos and cites territorial dispossession; the commission was tasked to assess land claims and facilitate regional dialogue.
claims.limitations: Official framing and mandate, not a measure of violence or conflict-resolution outcomes.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The decree frames territorial dispossession as an antecedent of the Mapuche–State conflict; it does not assert a climate pathway.

claims.locator: PDF p. 4, recitals 14°–16° on land-fund purchases and pending applications
claims.paraphrase: The resolution says 99.59% of Indigenous land-fund purchases through 2024 occurred in the four regions and were for Mapuche applicants; 1,131 applications remained pending when recommendations were delivered.
institutions: Ministry of Social Development and Family
claims.limitations: Administrative land-fund figures are not a count of all unresolved territorial claims.

search_audit.query: Chile official climate change vulnerability subnational Araucanía wildfire drought region report PDF government
search_audit.outcome: Opened the Indigenous vulnerability report and UNICEF wildfire situation report; found named Araucanía communities and named Valparaíso municipalities, but no Indigenous-disaggregated commune-level water-risk estimates.

search_audit.query: Chile Mapuche conflict climate drought wildfire violence official report climate change source
search_audit.outcome: The official resolution and Indigenous study document land/resource conflict context; neither establishes that climate change causes armed or political violence. UNICEF describes post-fire protection/security risks, not conflict-related violence.

search_audit.query: Chile conflict violence security disruption climate adaptation water infrastructure official report
search_audit.outcome: No inspected source showed ongoing territorial conflict or insecurity disrupting climate adaptation or water services; UNICEF's security findings were limited to the wildfire emergency response period.

search_audit.query: Chile climate adaptation resilience capacity municipalities Indigenous Mapuche water drought government report
search_audit.outcome: The DGA describes the formal 2025–2029 water adaptation plan, named pilot basins and municipal capacity tools; the Indigenous study provides workshop-identified capacities and proposed, not evaluated, measures.

gaps: No inspected source establishes a climate-change-to-armed/political-violence pathway in Chile; this is a search gap, not evidence of absence.
The Mapuche-specific climate chain is workshop-based and conceptual; public commune-level indicators disaggregated for Indigenous communities were not found.
No inspected source showed territorial insecurity disrupting ongoing climate adaptation or routine water services; UNICEF's reported safety concerns are tied to the February 2024 wildfire emergency.
The 2024 UNFCCC BTR PDF timed out and the official repository link for the water-plan PDF returned a cache miss; the accessible DGA plan summary was used for water-plan claims.
